Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 51 (appeal to National Commission and deposit)
Constitution of India - Articles 227 and 136
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: Section 67 confers a statutory appeal to the Supreme Court only against orders of the National Commission passed in exercise of its original jurisdiction under section 58(1)(a)(i) and (ii); no appeal is provided against an order made by the National Commission in an appeal under section 58(1)(a)(iii). The National Commission is a tribunal within the meaning of Article 227, and since no further statutory remedy exists, a writ petition under Article 227 before the High Court is maintainable against such an order. Access to the High Court is also more affordable and accessible to the litigant than invoking Article 136, which serves the object of meaningful access to justice; but the High Court must keep within the limited supervisory scope of Article 227 and not treat the petition as an appeal on merits.
metadatas.summary: The Supreme Court held that an order of the National Commission made in an appeal under section 58(1)(a)(iii) can be challenged by a writ petition under Article 227 before the High Court, because section 67 gives no statutory appeal against such orders and the National Commission is a tribunal subject to the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction. The consumer's appeal was dismissed and the matter remitted to the High Court to be decided on merits within the confined scope of Article 227.

metadatas.case_name: Bar of Indian Lawyers through its President Jasbir Singh Malik v. D.K. Gandhi PS National Institute of Communicable Diseases
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 2(42) (service; exclusion of service under a contract of personal service)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 2(7) (consumer), Section 2(11) (deficiency) and Section 2(47) (unfair trade practice)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(o)
Advocates Act, 1961
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: The object and purpose of the consumer legislation is to protect consumers against unfair trade practices and unethical business practices of traders, manufacturers and commercial service providers; it was not enacted to bring the professions within its net. A profession, requiring advanced education, specialised mental skill and adherence to an ethical code administered by its own regulator, stands on a different footing from business or trade, so that a professional cannot be equated with a businessman nor his client with a consumer in the statutory sense. The relationship between an advocate and his client is one of agency in which the client exercises a substantial measure of direction and control over the manner in which the advocate acts, and the advocate is bound by his client's instructions and owes fiduciary duties; such service is therefore rendered under 'a contract of personal service', which the definition of service in section 2(42) expressly excludes. Accordingly a complaint against an advocate alleging deficiency in service is not maintainable under the Act. The correctness of Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, in so far as it treats the professional services of medical practitioners as covered, was doubted and referred for consideration by a larger Bench, but that decision continues to hold the field until reconsidered.
metadatas.summary: The Supreme Court held that advocates' services are outside the Consumer Protection Act: the legislation targets traders and commercial service providers rather than the professions, and the advocate-client relationship is a contract of personal service expressly excluded from the definition of 'service'. A client's remedy for professional negligence therefore lies in a civil action or before the Bar Council, not in the consumer fora. The Court also doubted the reasoning of Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha and referred it to a larger Bench, so the position of medical professionals remains governed by Shantha for the present.

metadatas.case_name: Godrej Projects Development Ltd. v. Anil Karlekar
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 2(46) (unfair contract)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(r) (unfair trade practice)
Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Section 74 (penalty)
RERA Act, 2016
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: Forfeiture of earnest money that is reasonable in amount does not amount to a penalty within section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, but an unreasonable forfeiture does. Following the consistent view of the National Commission in DLF Ltd. v. Bhagwanti Narula, ten per cent of the Basic Sale Price is a reasonable amount liable to be forfeited as earnest money, and forfeiture of twenty per cent was disproportionate. Cases such as Satish Batra v. Sudhir Rawal and Desh Raj v. Rohtash Singh, which upheld forfeiture, involved parties bargaining on equal and reciprocal terms; where the agreement is ex facie one-sided and tilted in favour of the developer, permitting it to delay completion against nominal compensation while visiting the buyer with automatic cancellation and heavy forfeiture, such clauses are unfair and unreasonable, and their incorporation constitutes an unfair trade practice which the Court will not enforce against the consumer. Interest on the refund was, however, declined, because the cancellation was sought by the buyers on account of market conditions after possession had been validly offered, and not by reason of any default of the developer.
metadatas.summary: Buyers who refused an offered apartment because the market had fallen sought a full refund, while the builder claimed to forfeit twenty per cent of the Basic Sale Price. The Supreme Court held one-sided forfeiture clauses in builder-buyer agreements to be an unfair trade practice, fixed ten per cent of the Basic Sale Price as the reasonable measure of earnest money that may be forfeited, and reduced the forfeiture accordingly, directing refund of Rs. 34,04,170. Interest was refused because the buyers, not the developer, had occasioned the cancellation. This is the leading recent authority on earnest-money forfeiture and section 2(46) unfair contracts.

metadatas.case_name: Rutu Mihir Panchal v. Union of India
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 34(1) (jurisdiction of District Commission)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 47(1)(a)(i) (jurisdiction of State Commission)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 58(1)(a)(i) (jurisdiction of National Commission)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 2(7) (consumer)
Constitution of India - Article 14
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: Applying the twin test of permissible classification, consideration is integral both to the formation of the contract and to the statutory definition of 'consumer', and therefore furnishes an intelligible differentia; and the value of the consideration paid for the goods or service is more closely and readily relatable to the compensation properly payable than a self-assessed claim for damages, so that the classification bears a rational nexus with the object of the Act. A consumer has no unrestricted claim to compensation, the amount being always subject to determination by the forum, and keying jurisdiction to consideration guards against exaggerated and inflated claims while redistributing the caseload from an overburdened National Commission to the District and State Commissions. The Commissions also retain inherent power to prevent abuse by scrutinising overvalued claims. Sections 34, 47 and 58 are accordingly constitutional and not violative of Article 14.
metadatas.summary: The Supreme Court upheld the consideration-based test of pecuniary jurisdiction under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 against a challenge under Article 14 brought by claimants whose very large compensation claims arose from modest transactions. Consideration is a valid basis of classification because it is integral to the consumer relationship and is a more reliable proxy for compensation than a self-assessed claim, and the scheme serves the legitimate objects of curbing inflated claims and easing the National Commission's docket. The writ petition and appeal were dismissed, with a direction to the Central Consumer Protection Council and the Central Consumer Protection Authority to audit the working of the provisions and advise the Government on measures for effective redressal.

metadatas.case_name: Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(d) (consumer)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(o) (service)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(g) (deficiency)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 14(1)(d) (compensation)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 3 (Act not in derogation of any other law)
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: The definition of 'service' in section 2(1)(o) is expressed in the widest terms and, being consumer-oriented welfare legislation, must be construed liberally in favour of the consumer; housing construction and development activity undertaken for consideration falls squarely within it, and a statutory authority carrying on such activity is not exempt merely because it is a public body discharging statutory functions, for when it undertakes to build and allot houses for a price it renders a service like any other builder. An allottee who pays the price is therefore a consumer, and delay in delivering possession, defective or incomplete construction, or an illegal demand for additional payment constitutes a deficiency in service. The power to award compensation under section 14(1)(d) is wide enough to cover not merely pecuniary loss but harassment, mental agony and the consequences of arbitrary or capricious official action, and where the loss results from the misfeasance or oppressive conduct of an identified officer, the authority may recover the compensation so paid from that officer, since compensation ultimately borne by the public exchequer for an officer's malfeasance would otherwise burden the taxpayer.
metadatas.summary: The foundational decision bringing statutory development authorities and housing construction within the Consumer Protection Act. The Supreme Court read 'service' expansively, held that an authority allotting houses for consideration renders a service and that its allottees are consumers, treated delay, defective construction and illegal demands as deficiency, and recognised the power of the consumer fora to award compensation for harassment and mental agony, with liberty to the authority to recover such compensation from the erring officer personally.

metadatas.case_name: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(o) (service; exclusions for free service and contract of personal service)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(d) (consumer)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(g) (deficiency)
Indian Medical Council Act, 1956
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: Service rendered by a medical practitioner or hospital for a fee is 'service' within section 2(1)(o), for the definition excludes only service which is free of charge or given under a contract of personal service, and neither exclusion ordinarily applies. The expression 'contract of personal service' denotes a relationship of master and servant involving a right of the employer to control the manner of the work, and must be distinguished from a 'contract for personal service' under which a professional is engaged; a doctor consulted by a patient renders service under a contract for service, not of service, and the exclusion therefore does not apply. Where medical service is rendered entirely free of charge to everybody it falls outside the Act; but where a hospital charges some patients and renders free service to others, the free service is also covered, since the institution's charges sustain the whole activity; and where the charges are paid by an employer or under an insurance policy, the patient remains a beneficiary and hence a consumer. The existence of disciplinary control under the Medical Council legislation does not oust the jurisdiction of the consumer fora, and complexity of the issues is no reason to deny the statutory remedy.
metadatas.summary: The landmark ruling that brought the medical profession within consumer law. Paid medical service is 'service'; a doctor-patient engagement is a contract *for* service and not the excluded contract *of* personal service; wholly gratuitous service is outside the Act, but free treatment in a hospital that charges other patients is covered, as is treatment paid for by an employer or insurer. Note for currency: in Bar of Indian Lawyers v. D.K. Gandhi (2024) the Supreme Court doubted the reasoning of this decision and referred it to a larger Bench, but Shantha continues to govern medical services until reconsidered.

metadatas.case_name: Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(d) and the explanation thereto (commercial purpose; self-employment)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(f) (defect)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 2(7) and its Explanation (corresponding provision)
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: Whether goods have been bought for a commercial purpose is always a question of fact turning on the purpose for which the purchase was made, and not on the size, turnover or statutory registration of the buyer's enterprise. Goods bought and used for carrying on an activity on a large scale with a view to earning profit are bought for a commercial purpose and the buyer is not a consumer. The explanation carves out a narrow exception for a person who buys and uses the goods himself, exclusively for earning his livelihood by means of self-employment, and it is the character of self-employment for livelihood, rather than the label of small-scale industry, that attracts the exception; the employment of a small number of assistants does not by itself take a case outside it. The consumer fora are not the forum for adjudicating claims of loss of profit arising out of a commercial venture.
metadatas.summary: The leading authority on the 'commercial purpose' exclusion. The Supreme Court held that whether a purchase is for a commercial purpose depends on the purpose of the buyer and not on the scale or registration of his business, and that the self-employment explanation protects only one who buys and uses the goods himself exclusively to earn his livelihood. A small-scale industry that bought a machine to manufacture for profit was therefore not a consumer. The same reasoning now applies to the identical Explanation to section 2(7) of the 2019 Act.

metadatas.case_name: Bharathi Knitting Co. v. DHL Worldwide Express Courier
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(g) (deficiency)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(o) (service)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 14(1)(d) (compensation)
Indian Contract Act, 1872
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: Where the parties have, by a contract freely entered into, agreed to limit the liability of the service provider to a specified amount, that limitation governs the claim, and the consumer fora adjudicating a complaint arising out of that very contract are bound by it and cannot award compensation in excess of the agreed ceiling. A party who has signed the contract and accepted its terms cannot claim damages beyond the stipulated limit merely because the loss actually suffered is greater. The position is different where the term is itself vitiated, and the remedy of a claimant who disputes the limitation on such grounds lies elsewhere; the consumer fora, whose jurisdiction arises from the contract, must give effect to it as it stands.
metadatas.summary: The Supreme Court held that a contractual clause limiting a courier's liability for a lost consignment binds both the consumer and the consumer fora, so that compensation cannot exceed the agreed ceiling even if the actual business loss was larger. The decision is the principal authority on limitation-of-liability clauses in consumer contracts, and is to be read today alongside the later line of cases on unfair contracts and one-sided terms, and with section 2(46) of the 2019 Act.

metadatas.case_name: Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjol Ahluwalia
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(d) (consumer, including a beneficiary of service)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(o) (service)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(g) (deficiency)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 14(1)(d) (compensation)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 2(7) (corresponding definition of consumer)
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: The definition of consumer is wide enough to cover both the person who hires or avails of the service for consideration and the beneficiary of that service, so that where parents engage a hospital for the treatment of their minor child, the parents are consumers as the persons who availed of the service and the child is a consumer as its beneficiary; both may therefore maintain a claim in the same complaint. Compensation may accordingly be awarded to the child for the injury and lifelong incapacity caused to him, and separately to the parents for the acute mental agony and the life-long care and anguish that the tragedy has visited upon them. A hospital is liable for the negligence of the staff it employs and for allowing a person without the requisite qualification to administer treatment without the supervision of a qualified doctor.
metadatas.summary: A child suffered irreversible brain damage after a nurse administered an injection intravenously without medical supervision. The Supreme Court held that both the parents, who engaged and paid the hospital, and the child, as beneficiary, were consumers entitled to claim in one complaint, and upheld separate awards to the child for the injury and to the parents for mental agony. It remains the leading authority on the beneficiary limb of the definition of consumer and on compensation for mental agony in medical negligence.

metadatas.case_name: Charan Singh v. Healing Touch Hospital
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 14(1)(d) (compensation for loss or injury due to negligence)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(g) (deficiency)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 39(1)(d) (corresponding power to award compensation, including punitive damages)
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: The power to award compensation is intended to provide real and effective redress, and the amount awarded must be adequate and commensurate with the loss and injury actually suffered; a token or nominal award defeats the object of the legislation, while an unreasonably high award is equally to be avoided. In quantifying compensation the forum must apply its mind to the facts and take into account the several heads of loss, including the expense already incurred and to be incurred on remedial treatment, the pain, suffering and mental agony caused, the loss of earnings or earning capacity, and the harassment occasioned, and must strike a balance between the claim and the capacity of the opposite party so that the award is neither a windfall nor an empty gesture. Compensation so assessed also serves to deter the negligent provider from repeating such conduct, and the forum should record how it has arrived at the figure.
metadatas.summary: Finding the compensation awarded for negligent surgery inadequate, the Supreme Court held that awards under the Act must be commensurate with the injury and not token, and set out the heads a consumer forum should weigh in quantification: expenses incurred and to be incurred, pain and suffering, mental agony, loss of earning capacity and harassment, balanced so as to be neither a windfall nor illusory. It is the standard authority cited on the assessment of compensation in consumer cases.

metadatas.case_name: Dr. J.J. Merchant v. Shrinath Chaturvedi
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 13(2)(a) (time for filing version) and Section 13(4) (powers of the fora)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(g) and Section 2(1)(o)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 38(2)(a) and Section 38(9) (corresponding provisions)
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: The Act was enacted to provide speedy and inexpensive redress, and the consumer fora, which are presided over by judicially trained persons and are empowered to summon and examine witnesses, to receive evidence on affidavit and to requisition expert reports, are fully competent to decide complaints of medical negligence; the mere complexity of the questions involved is no ground for refusing to exercise jurisdiction or for driving the consumer to a civil suit, since that would frustrate the purpose of the statute. The period prescribed for filing the written version, namely thirty days extendable by not more than fifteen days, is mandatory and the fora have no power to extend it beyond the outer limit, the legislative intent being to prevent the delay which the statute was designed to avoid.
metadatas.summary: The Supreme Court rejected the contention that medical negligence claims are too complex for the consumer fora, holding that they are competent to try such cases with the aid of affidavit and expert evidence, and that relegating consumers to civil suits would defeat the Act's promise of speedy redress. It also held the thirty plus fifteen day limit for filing the written version to be mandatory. On this second point the law was unsettled for years by the contrary view in Topline Shoes, until the Constitution Bench in New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Hilli Multipurpose Cold Storage (2020) affirmed that the limit is mandatory.

metadatas.case_name: Topline Shoes Ltd. v. Corporation Bank
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 13(2)(a) (time for filing version)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 13(3A) (endeavour to decide within three or five months)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 38(2)(a) (corresponding provision)
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: The provision prescribing thirty days, extendable by such period not exceeding fifteen days as may be granted, does not provide for any penal consequence on failure to file the version within that time, and it is intended to expedite and not to defeat the hearing of the case on its merits; the requirement is therefore directory rather than mandatory, and the forum retains a measure of discretion, to be exercised for sufficient reason and consistently with the principles of natural justice, to accept a version filed beyond the outer limit. Important note on currency: this view was doubted in Dr. J.J. Merchant v. Shrinath Chaturvedi and the conflict was resolved against Topline Shoes by the Constitution Bench in New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Hilli Multipurpose Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. (2020), which held that the period is mandatory and cannot be extended beyond forty-five days; the reasoning of Topline Shoes therefore no longer represents the law on this point.
metadatas.summary: The Supreme Court held that the thirty plus fifteen day period for filing a written version under section 13(2)(a) was directory and not mandatory, since the provision imposes no penalty for default and is meant to speed up rather than shut out a hearing on merits, leaving the forum a discretion to condone delay for sufficient reason. This position was later overruled: the Constitution Bench in New India Assurance v. Hilli Multipurpose Cold Storage (2020) held the limit mandatory. The case is retained here for the development of the law and should not be cited as the current rule.

metadatas.case_name: Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 14(1)(d) (compensation)
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 2(1)(g) (deficiency) and Section 2(1)(o) (service)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 39(1)(c) and (d) (refund with interest; compensation)
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: Compensation under section 14(1)(d) must be assessed on the facts of each case and cannot be granted mechanically at a uniform rate of interest, and the observations in Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta were not intended to lay down a flat rate of eighteen per cent for all cases. Where an allottee's money has been retained without delivery of possession, interest is awardable by way of restitution to compensate him for the deprivation of the use of his money, and the rate must reflect the circumstances; where in addition the allottee has suffered harassment, or has been given possession of a different or inferior property, or has had to bear escalation, a further sum may be awarded under distinct heads, each supported by reasons. The forum must therefore identify the heads of loss and quantify each, rather than apply a single conventional figure.
metadatas.summary: Correcting the practice of awarding a flat eighteen per cent interest in development-authority cases, the Supreme Court held that compensation must be computed case by case on the material before the forum: interest by way of restitution for money withheld, assessed at a rate appropriate to the facts, with any further amounts for harassment or for allotment of different property awarded separately and with reasons. It clarified that Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta laid down no uniform rate.

metadatas.case_name: State Bank of India v. B.S. Agricultural Industries (I)
sections: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - Section 24A (limitation period; condonation of delay)
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Section 69 (corresponding limitation provision)
metadatas.ratio_decidendi: Section 24A is peremptory in terms: it expressly commands that the forum shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years of the accrual of the cause of action, and the proviso permits a complaint to be entertained thereafter only if the complainant satisfies the forum that he had sufficient cause for the delay and the forum records its reasons for condoning it. The provision therefore casts a duty on the consumer forum to examine, whether or not the point is raised by the opposite party, whether the complaint has been filed within the prescribed period, and it has no jurisdiction to entertain a barred complaint in the absence of an application for condonation supported by sufficient cause and a reasoned order condoning the delay. A decision on the merits of a complaint which was time-barred and in which delay was never condoned cannot be sustained.
metadatas.summary: The Supreme Court held the two-year limitation in section 24A to be mandatory and jurisdictional: a consumer forum must satisfy itself on limitation of its own motion, even if the opposite party does not plead it, and can entertain a stale complaint only where sufficient cause is shown and delay is condoned by a reasoned order. This is the leading authority on limitation in consumer proceedings and applies with equal force to section 69 of the 2019 Act.
